idiom_name: role interfaces + embedded forwarder struct + mutex-guarded role map on the core
implementation_notes: Go's implicit interfaces and promoted methods remove the forwarding boilerplate the classic ComponentRole exists for: a role struct embeds a small forwarder, and because promoted methods join the method set (Go spec, Struct types) the role satisfies both the role interface and the core interface, while embedded interfaces compose capabilities (the ReadWriter style) when a client needs several. What remains hand-written is the dynamic part: the core keeps a role map keyed by role id or reflect.Type behind a sync.Mutex/sync.RWMutex, exposes AddRole/GetRole/HasRole, and instantiates roles through a constructor table so new roles still enter without changing the core. Where the role set is known at compile time, explicit fields or a type switch are simpler than a registry.
pitfalls: A role map read and written concurrently is a data race; guard it with sync.RWMutex or sync.Map, or document single-threaded use.
An interface value holding a typed nil pointer is not equal to nil; GetRole must return (Role, bool) and callers must test the bool, not the interface value.
reflect.TypeOf keys roles by concrete type, so two differently parametrized roles of the same type need an explicit specification key instead.
